rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Ecological adaptation refers to the structural, physiological, and behavioural features that allow an organism to survive in its environment. Hydrophytes (water plants) have aerenchyma, floating leaves, reduced roots, and thin cuticles for aquatic life. Xerophytes (dry-land plants) have thick cuticles, spines (modified leaves), succulent stems, deep roots, and CAM photosynthesis for arid conditions.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Hydrophyte adaptations: aerenchyma + floating leaves + reduced roots + upper-surface stomata + thin cuticle
Xerophyte adaptations: thick cuticle + spines (modified leaves) + succulent stem + deep roots + CAM photosynthesis
CAM photosynthesis: fix CO2 at night (malic acid) → decarboxylate by day (reduced water loss)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Hydrophytes have AERENCHYMA (air spaces) for gas exchange; xerophytes have reduced surface area to conserve water.  ·  Cacti's "spines" are modified LEAVES (to reduce water loss); the stem is the photosynthetic organ (succulent).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a clear hydrophyte vs xerophyte comparison with specific adaptations.  ·  The cactus spines (modified leaves) and succulent stem are key exam points.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Hydrophyte (water hyacinth): aerenchyma, floating leaves, reduced roots, stomata on upper surface, thin cuticle.  ·  Xerophyte (cactus): thick cuticle, spines (modified leaves), succulent stem, deep roots, CAM photosynthesis.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Xerophytes often use CAM photosynthesis (open stomata at night to reduce water loss); hydrophytes use the C3 pathway with stomata on the upper surface.  ·  Hydrophytes may have REDUCED roots (they float; roots are for anchorage, not water uptake).

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Adaptation types (structural, physiological, behavioural)  ·  Hydrophytes (aerenchyma, floating leaves)  ·  Xerophytes (thick cuticle, spines, CAM)  ·  Mesophytes

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Adaptation: structural, physiological, behavioural features for survival.  ·  Hydrophytes: aerenchyma, floating leaves, reduced roots, thin cuticle.  ·  Xerophytes: thick cuticle, spines (modified leaves), succulent stem, deep roots, CAM photosynthesis.  ·  Mesophytes: moderate moisture; intermediate adaptations.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Cacti can survive with as little as 10% of the water a typical plant needs.  ·  Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) is an invasive species in many tropical water bodies, including Nepal.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Define CAM photosynthesis and its significance.  ·  Differentiate structural, physiological, and behavioural adaptations.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Mesophyte (oak, rhododendron): moderate water; normal cuticle, normal leaves, roots in moist soil.  ·  Structural adaptation: cactus spines (reduced leaf area).

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The air spaces in the tissues of a hydrophyte are called: → B  ·  The "spines" of a cactus are modified: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Ecological adaptation: the structural, physiological, and behavioural features that allow an organism to survive in a particular environment.  ·  Adaptation types: structural (body form), physiological (internal processes), behavioural (activities).  ·  Hydrophytes (water plants): adapted to aquatic life; examples: water hyacinth (Nymphaea lotus), lotus, Vallisneria.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Water hyacinth adaptations  ·  Adaptation is evolutionary (population level), not individual (acclimatisation).  ·  Hydrophytes: gas exchange via aerenchyma; Xerophytes: water conservation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: CAM: open stomata at night, close by day.  ·  Adaptation is a POPULATION-LEVEL feature (evolution over generations), NOT an individual changing during its life.  ·  Acclimatisation (short-term, individual adjustment) is different from adaptation (long-term, evolutionary).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Physiological adaptation: CAM photosynthesis in cacti.  ·  CAM photosynthesis (xerophytes) is a frequent physiological question.  ·  Note that adaptation is evolutionary, not individual (acclimatisation is individual).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Memorise 4 hydrophyte adaptations and 4 xerophyte adaptations.  ·  Learn the cactus adaptations (spines, succulent stem, deep roots, CAM).  ·  Explain CAM photosynthesis and its significance.
